chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
title: Being 'stuck in a time warp' and today's pop
summary: She doesn't know currently popular tunes; Hughes notes contemporary singers using older repertoire.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Anyway, I interrupted you before, and in a sense I contradicted you and I really didn't mean to do that. You say you are stuck in a time warp.
So I want to let you finish that and tell us what you mean by that.

What I mean by that is, I don't know too many currently popular tunes. I don't care to hear them, and even if I accidentally hear them, I haven't heard anything good in a long time, you know, that appealed to me. The reason I say that is I must be stuck somewhere, you know as late as 1950 or something like that because I don't hear too much good music. So I feel a little ancient. But I don't mind being ancient.
Well, the character of pop music has changed and I think we did talk a little bit about that earlier. But there are contemporary singers, contemporary swing or jazz singers, however you call them
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

who do work in their own way the same kind of repertoire as was popular in the 1930s. Do you listen to those? Yeah, especially if they're doing those kinds of songs. You don't hear too many of them though. I'm trying to think of the last singer that I heard that was considered the new singer of our type. I can't recall. Alot of the new singers are into gospel, the disco and the hustle beat, and I don't hear too much lyrics, too much melody, all I hear is thump, thump, thump, you know. And I don't even hear the lyrics.

You got to be in to know what they're talking about. It's like a cult. If you listen to the lyrics the lyrics don't make much sense to you if you're square, but if you're in then you'll know what they're talking about.
